utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dan Saxon, April Carter, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Novak Lukic, and Gregor Guy-Smith appearing on behalf of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Carter will call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Colonel Pyers Tucker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Pyers Tucker.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There may be some discussion with regard to Colonel Pyers Tucker's testimony. I believe that Ms. Carter believes this is more appropriately a discussion which is had outside of his presence. I, quite frankly, have no opinion in that regard, but I want to raise the issue because she raised it with me informally. This deals with the contours and extent of his testimony. It's my understanding that it is the Prosecution's intent to have Pyers Tucker testify with regard to matters that are pre-indictment and not with regard to matters that deal with the indictment period. And therefore, we would object on those grounds because of the issue of relevance. But above and beyond that, there's also a question as to what subject matters the Prosecution intends on having Mr. Tucker testify with regard to. And in that regard, if one were to review the 65 ter summary as it relates to Pyers Tucker, it is my understanding that his testimony would be discrete and limited to those matters concerning Sarajevo. The reason I take that position is because the Prosecution indicates that, among other things - and I'm just going to get to the guts of what the Prosecution says with regard to his 65 ter witness summary. "He met Galic at least once and was involved in a number of instances where protests were lodged inter alia because of the shelling and sniping of civilians." That of course would deal with Sarajevo. "His testimony will be particularly relevant as to command and control and notice. The witness worked as the assistant to General Morillon. The witness will provide pre-indictment background as to the situation in Sarajevo. The witness attended meetings with the military leadership of both warring factions including General Mladic." "He will discuss the assassination of BiH deputy prime minister Trialik [phoen] by a Bosnian Serb soldier in the presence of UNPROFOR officials." And we know from testimony that we have already heard, that occurred in the Sarajevo region. "Paragraphs of the indictment to which his testimony pertains. Paragraphs of the indictment is 41 and background to the situation in Sarajevo when Tucker took over and when he left." And if we review paragraph 41 of the indictment it states: "In this time-period, the commanders of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps of the VRS, General Stanislav Galic (10 September 1992 to 10 August 1994) and General Dragomir Milosevic (10 August 1994 to November 1995) and their superior General Ratko Mladic, continued in extensive shelling and sniping attack on Sarajevo, mostly from positions in the hills surrounding the city." And that is the extent of the allegation as it relates to paragraph 41. And I believe that the testimony that is to be adduced from this witness is specific in nature and relates to only Sarajevo. The reason I raise this concern is because the proofing note that I have received in large measure deals with the subject matter other than Sarajevo; it deals with Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I'm not quite sure what this whole speech is, is it an objection? Are you raising --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know what you are objecting to. Can I suggest that as the situation arises, you stand up and object. I really don't know what to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure, I was just trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know what to ask Madam Carter to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I was trying to be some assistance to the Chamber because this issue is going to come up, and I wanted to give you some information concerning the parameters and contours of what the concern would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Guy-Smith. Unfortunately it's just too much information for us to digest for purposes of an objection. Can I suggest that you raise your objection as and when the objection arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure, not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, not to be disrespectful to -- from Your Honours most recent ruling, I do understand what Mr. Guy-Smith is indicating, he is reciting the 65 ter summary that was submitted during the pre-trial brief stage of this case in which we had limited the 65 ter summary solely to Sarajevo. However, there was a motion on 1 May 2008, which was decided by this Court on 4 June 2008 which expanded the 65 ter summary of Pyers Tucker to include Srebrenica. I can recite the 65 ter summary in full, but I would guide Mr. Guy-Smith as well as the Court to the full summary that is dated 1 May 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. May I suggest also that you give that answer to Mr. Guy-Smith as and when he stands up to object.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. And when Mr. Guy-Smith began his objection, he was also speaking to the pre-indictment evidence that will be given by this witness. I had suggested that we deal with this before the witness comes in because the way I intend to respond to that objection would be inappropriate in front of this witness. And given the fact that the witness's entire testimony does relate to pre-indictment period, I believe that it would be appropriate to respond to that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Colonel Tucker will testify to the 1992 to 1993 siege of Sarajevo and ethnic cleansing of Bosnia's eastern municipalities by the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me. May I interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you responding to the objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the pre-indictment area?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Following worldwide condemnation of these actions, the United Nations passed numerous resolutions. Perisic was on notice of these crimes yet he continued --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's request: Could you please read slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly. Following worldwide condemnation of these actions, the United Nations passed numerous resolutions. Perisic was on notice of these crimes, yet he continued Serbia's assistance to the VRS once appointed Chief of the General Staff of the VJ in August 1993. This continued assistance led to the continued campaign of shelling and sniping in Sarajevo and the ultimate massacre at Srebrenica in July 1995. Your Honours, I would argue that pre-indictment evidence may be admitted to establish pattern, a specific element of a crime, or to provide context. Admissibility turns on the finding that the evidence has probative value to the indictment period. Historically, this Chamber has admitted pre-indictment evidence of notice and pattern. This evidence has been admitted through adjudicated facts, witness testimony, and exhibits. And admitted adjudicated facts concerning Sarajevo, the Trial Chamber found that evidence which established a consistent pattern of conduct proceeding the indictment might be relevant to prove Perisic's mens rea. Later, the Trial Chamber has accepted the testimonies of General John Wilson and Aernout Van Lynden related to the 1993 and 1992 as evidence of notice. Most recently, the Trial Chamber admitted as evidence the notice of the reports of the Special Rapporteur of the commission on human rights spanning 27 October 1992 to 22 August 1995. As the arguments related to the relevance of Sarajevo have been previously set out, I will focus the remainder of my argument on Srebrenica. As detailed in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, the prior ethnic cleansing was antecedent to the 1995 massacre charged in counts 9 to 13 of the indictment. The fate of Srebrenica was sealed upon the establishment of the strategic objectives to be carried out by the VRS, which included the separation of the Serbs from the non-Serbs and the elimination of the border between Serbia and Republika Srpska. Cleansing operations began which were to be realisations of these objectives.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, the interpreters are complain that you are reading too fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure how reading that whole passage that you are reading is in response to the objection. Aren't you able just to tell us that you know according to that document of which the Defence has notice, if they do, that in fact you are supposed to cover the pre-indictment period.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding of the Mr. Guy-Smith's objection is twofold. One that the 65 ter summary bound us only to Sarajevo, and two, that the evidence in full was irrelevant because it dealt with pre-indictment information. I responded first to the objection in regards to the 65 ter summary, and now I'm dealing with the relevance of pre-indictment information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was my understanding of what she was responding to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You may proceed then, if you understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cleansing operations began which we were to be realisations of these objectives. By 19 November 1992, Directive 4 was issued stating the enemy groups in the wider area of Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica, and Cerska have not been totally routed, and the decision was made to cleanse the territory of Republika Srpska. The Drina Corps was tasked with forcing the Muslim population to leave Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde. Further, paragraph 55 of the indictment states that 1993 saw the International Court of Justice and the United Nations issuing orders and resolutions condemning these cleansing operations and calling for an end of hostilities. By 8 April 1993, the International Court of Justice ordered the FRY to take all immediate measures in its power to prevent genocide. The UN reaffirmed this order and noted that the actions in Eastern Bosnia involved unlawful attacks on civilians and called for the FRY to immediately cease the supply of military arms, equipment, and services to the VRS. While serving as the military assistant to the commander of the United Nations protective force from October 1992 to March 1993, Colonel Tucker met with the Serbian and Bosnian Serb leadership and witnessed the ethnic cleansing of the eastern municipalities. This cleansing operation was accomplished with the act of support of the FRY including artillery fire from Serbia, air support, restriction of UNPROFOR's movement, and the provision of salaries for VRS. Colonel Tucker is uniquely placed to describe the cleansing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: -- the cleansing campaign both as an observer as well as a person in contemporaneous contact with the principal actors. The witness met with Radovan Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down, slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: -- and Ratko Mladic in November 1992. At that meeting, Karadzic explained to him in graphic detail the plans in store for the Muslim population. Taking a census map, Karadzic explained that all territories which were 50 per cent or more Serbian populated would be cleansed, stating that they had no desire to live with the Turks. This operation began in the spring of 1992. In March 1993, Colonel Tucker met with Colonel Vinko Pandurevic future 30th Personnel Centre member. Colonel Pandurevic had maps on his wall that detailed a systematic cleansing of the eastern municipalities including dates and lines depicting how far the advance had progressed. Later as commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Colonel Pandurevic was one of the commanders responsible for the July 1995 massacre. Colonel Tucker met with several additional commanders who would eventually be members of the 30th Personnel Centre as detailed in Schedule E of the indictment. Colonel Tucker met with General Ratko Mladic, Major-Generals Zdravko Tolimir and Lieutenant-Colonel-General Milan Gvero. These men would also later be principals in the 1995 massacre. As Colonel Tucker's evidence is relevant and probative to the issues of notice, foreseeability, and pattern related to Sarajevo and Srebrenica, it is admissible and thus we would be requested to lead this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may respond, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, starting with the last comment made on lines 22 through 25 on page 8 and line 1 of page 9, there is no evidence presented of that in this case, and there is no proof of that in any case as of yet. I'd like to start with the very beginning of what Ms. Carter said with regard to Mr. Perisic being on notice, and specifically she said on page 5 at line 12: "Perisic was on notice of these crimes, yet he continued Serbia's assistance to the VRS once appointed Chief of General Staff of the VJ in August 1993." That may well be the theory of the Prosecution, but there is no evidence of that. There have been a number of occasions in which the issue of nexus between the knowledge of Mr. Perisic and the act that was being complained of or was attempted to be proved has been put into question, specifically with regards to such issues as the issue of foreseeability. And this Chamber has previously ruled that where there is no nexus, that such evidence is inappropriate and inadmissible. I understand the Prosecution's theory here, but with regard to the factual predicates upon which they presently rely, there are a number of glaring holes and failures of proof. And above and beyond that, once again there has been no showing of a nexus between those events that occurred prior to General Perisic's obtaining the position of Chief of Staff and his knowledge of them. And in the absence of that, what the Chamber is being asked to do is hear evidence which is highly speculative with regard to what Perisic knew, what Perisic was aware of and the absence of any hard evidence, and the absence of any proof. And unless the Prosecution is in a position to make an offer of proof whereby they can establish such a link, I would submit, as I did at the outset, that this evidence is irrelevant to the charges here. Maybe in some other trial they may not be. But to this case, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution calls Colonel Pyers Tucker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we are waiting for Mr. Tucker, is there a possibility of reducing the temperature in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: While we are waiting, with regard to the response made by Ms. Carter concerning the 65 ter, I do stand corrected, I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have ruled on the objection, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I was referring to the second part of that which you said that when the issue came up in the event that I felt it necessary to object when the specific issue came up, so I'm taking care of that to expedite proceedings and also to acknowledge what my opponent said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're sorry we took time to call you, dealing with some other administrative matters. May you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tucker. You may be seated. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Colonel Tucker, can you please introduce yourself to the Court.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: My name is Pyers Tucker. I was a British Army officer from 1976 through to 1997 when I left the British Army. During the time 1992 to 1993, I served as a United Nations officer on secondment from the British Army in Bosnia as part of United Nations BH command. During that time, I was the personal staff officer of General Morillon. And as such, my main responsibility was to arrange for meetings between General Morillon and the various warring factions in Bosnia in order to try and execute the mission which the general, General Morillon, was obligated with from Security Council. During that time, I took the minutes of many meetings, and I drafted reports for General Morillon which were then sent from Bosnia, from Sarajevo headquarters, to the UN headquarters in Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, at this point I would interject. He was asked to introduce himself. He now is engaged in talking about his day-to-day work. The narrative form of his answer is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to begin at the inception of your career. Can you please describe what was your professional background and training in the British military?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: In the British Army, I was in the artillery. And my training was the same training as all officers receive in the British Army but then in particular I received training in artillery matters as an artillery officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How did you become a member of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The headquarters where I was serving in Germany was part of NATO, and it was based in Moenchengladbach and that headquarters was appointed to form the corps of the headquarters of the newly-formed United Nations Bosnia-Herzegovina command. And as an officer of the headquarters, I was sent to the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why was the Bosnia-Herzegovina command established?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: In July/August 1992, UNHCR identified that if nothing was done it was believed that over the winter of 1992 to 1993, I forget the exact figures, but it was something like 1.2 million people were at risk of dying from starvation unless something was done. And as a result of that, about ten countries agreed in August 1992 to form this United Nations Bosnia-Herzegovina command and contributed a total of at that time about 7.000 soldiers in order to be deployed into Bosnia in order to facilitate UN Security Council resolution whose objective was the facilitation of the supply of humanitarian aid to those in need. I can't remember exactly details, but that was the essence of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The supply of humanitarian aid to those in need, was that your sole mandate as members of the Bosnia-Herzegovina command?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That was the sole mandate.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. You were describing before your specific duties and responsibilities, and you indicated that you often attended meetings. Can you please tell the Court how many meetings did you have during your time in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I was in Bosnia-Herzegovina for just under six months. And in that that time I took the minutes of about 190 meetings; in other words, just over a meeting a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt, Madam Carter, just to understand your previous question. When you say, That was your sole mandate, was that the sole mandate of UNPROFOR or was that the sole mandate of some other ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was -- I cannot recall what the mandate of UNPROFOR as a whole was, but the mandate of BH command in Bosnia was the delivery of humanitarian aid to those in need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: BH command in Bosnia, BH command of what army or whose ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The BH command in Bosnia was the force deployed in Bosnia of which General Morillon was the commander. General Morillon was reported to, was subordinate to General Nambiar who was the commander of UNPROFOR which was based in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The meetings that you were setting up, who were they with?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The meetings were primarily with the warring factions. In other words, it was with the Bosnian Muslims, in other words, the Presidency, and their representatives inside Sarajevo and in other areas outside. It was with the Bosnian Serbs both military and political parlay and areas around Sarajevo and occasionally also with the Bosnian Croats. That was the vast majority of the meetings, though there were also meetings outside of Bosnia in Croatia and in Serbia, as in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you were meeting in Belgrade, who were you meeting with?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We met in Belgrade once with a group of Serb army officers in the Serb army headquarters in Belgrade. And we later met with Milosevic and a group of people at Milosevic's palace.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have a time-frame for the meetings you are referring to, since there are so many of them it might be of assistance, times of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Narrowing to your meetings in Belgrade, can you tell me when you met with these individuals?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The first meeting with a group of senior Serb army officers was around January 1993, and the meeting with Milosevic was around 25 or 26 March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Backing up a bit, you indicated that you also met with Bosnian Serb leadership, both political and military. Can you please tell us who you were meeting with?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The -- the only name who I have from the meeting in January was General Panic, and there were a group of about six or seven colonels and other colonels and generals in the meeting as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we may have -- misunderstanding each other. When you indicated you met with General Panic, are you indicating that he was a Bosnian Serb officer?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No, no. Sorry, I understood your question to be about Serb officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And initially it was, but then I actually moved on to Bosnian Serb officers. My apologies. Okay, moving to Bosnian Serb military and political figures that you met, who did you meet with?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We met with most of the senior Bosnian Serb officers starting with General Mladic, General Milovanovic, General Galic, General Gvero, and another 15 or 20 various generals and colonels. I would have to look at my minutes if you wanted me to find the names of all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any of the political leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, met with Karadzic, met with Madam Plavsic, met with - who is the guy who committed suicide? - Professor Koljevic. And then in various towns and villages met with local political leaders. Also met with -- with the president of the Bosnian Serb Assembly and the -- again, I would need to look in my notes to recall the names of all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when did you first meet Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I first met Karadzic in October 1992 just before he went to Geneva. He was in Geneva at the end of October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When did he return from Geneva?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but it would have been a couple of weeks later, because we met him again in Pale in November.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In the meeting in Pale, what did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We had a number of meetings with Karadzic over those weeks, and one of the first meetings in Pale where -- this was the first time that we, the new UN BH command, were meeting with Karadzic, General Mladic, with Koljevic, and a number of other -- I think Gvero was there as well. And Karadzic and General Mladic were at pains to try and explain historical background as they saw it, and one of the things that they did was get out a map which showed the ethnic distribution of Bosnia according to a recently completed census. And what they explained to General Morillon was that they had no intention to seize land which did not belong to them. And that they identified land that belonged to them as being land where more than 50 per cent of the population was Bosnian Serb. And that they did not want to live with -- together with the Bosnian Muslims. They had suffered enough whenever they were governed by other people. They wanted to live their own lives, separate from the Bosnian Muslims and --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And if I can call up 65 ter 9233.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, right before we go into this, I would at this time, based upon the proofing note that we've received, request a full copy of Colonel Tucker's personal diary which is not in your possession. I understand it's in his possession. We have some extracts of it, but there's obviously information in his personal diary that we do not have. And considering some of the subject matter that's just been raised, it would be appropriate for the Defence to have the entire diary so that we can review it for purposes of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the diary as was stated by Mr. Guy-Smith is not in our possession. However, it is in the possession of Colonel Tucker. I would not believe it would be the Prosecution's call as to whether that should be provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm requesting the diary in all fairness at this time so that we have the -- a basis upon which we can make a determination with regard to those historical facts that Colonel Tucker is alluding to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps I would ask Colonel Tucker if he would be willing to provide the Prosecution so a copy could be made of as a matter of courtesy. And if he doesn't feel that's appropriate, then we can move from that position. But that's where I'd start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what this diary is all about. We've asked for 65 ter 9233 to come up. Does this diary have anything to do with the 65 ter 9233?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This diary may well have something to do with -- no, to do with 9233, it does not. It has to do with some of the testimony that he just gave. With regard to 65 ter 9233, I don't know whether that's on our list, but I'm not -- that's a different issue. So before the witness examines that document, perhaps we could have a discussion about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, let me find out, so you are just making a request to Mr. Tucker to avail you his -- a copy of his diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You can sort that with Mr. Tucker. It doesn't call for a ruling from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But the difficulty is I'm not in a position to be able to talk to Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can do so when you start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But I'm -- if that's the case, then I will be asking the Court for an adjournment because I don't have his diary and I won't be in a position to review his diary before the cross-examination. And I'd rather not truncate the examination, so I'm trying to figure out a way of expediting the matter, which is why I'm raising it now. I'm trying to be more efficient, not less, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand. But the trouble is that the Bench doesn't know anything about this diary. This topic of a diary just pops up; I don't know where it comes from. And is it part of the pleadings? Has it ever been mentioned in the documents that have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's been mentioned in his testimony when he said he was referring to his, I believe he calls them his notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now you are asking for his diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would have to take a look at my minutes. Perhaps it would be, I believe the word "diary" and "minutes" are interchangeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do not think so. I think minutes are minutes and a diary is a diary. A diary notes your appointments and minutes are a record of what takes place in a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have a different understanding of the language there than you do, but that's okay. I'm asking for in whatever form he has memorialised information concerning his impressions of meetings that he had with the individuals that he has mentioned thus far in his testimony, number one. Number two, I'm requesting memorialisation in whatever form it is, whether it be in minutes, a diary, a notebook, or any other information above and beyond those individuals that he has specifically referred to for the period of time that he was the assistant to General Morillon and acting in that capacity he was a scrivener.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He was a?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Scrivener, one who takes notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Carter, it looks like the request is slightly different. I don't know whether you have any response to that. At least I understand it differently from a diary, the request for a diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that Mr. Guy-Smith took that word because that is how I put it in the proofing note. What is in the possession of Colonel Tucker that he reviewed during our proofing section is a hard-back book that did take all of the notes of meetings. And so I use the term diary, but we are talking about the same book that Mr. Guy-Smith is requesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. But what is your response to his request? He is asking for whatever form in which he memorialised what information he had concerning the meetings that he had with the various people during the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document -- the item that he is asking for was not in the possession of the Prosecution. We have previously taken extracts and disclosed those over the years. The item is the personal property of Colonel Tucker. To the extent that Colonel Tucker is willing to have that photocopied in its entirety, we certainly would have no objection to that. I've spoke within Ms. Javier, she has indicated that if the staff would like to deliver - because we are in the same position as Mr. Guy-Smith, we can't talk to the witness either - if the witness would be willing to provide it, Ms. Javier would be happy to photocopy it for the benefit of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, do you -- I'm sure you've heard what has been talked about, what is your response? Are you inclined to release your diary or book, record, whatever it is, or are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Providing that I get them back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I guess you would get them back.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly. So whenever it is convenient, I suppose at the court break if we can -- or actually at the end of testimony today that way we can make photocopies in the event that Colonel Tucker might need them during his testimony today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. And obviously if he is going to be asked about them, he needs to have his original, copies should be made for the the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether -- is the intention to tender those documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, they're not exhibits on the Prosecution's list. I don't know if Mr. Guy-Smith intends to tender them or what he might do with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May an arrangement be made that copies be made of Mr. Tucker's book.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Your Honour, I -- unfortunately when I called up the 65 ter number before I transposed numbers, the 65 ter that I'm actually looking for is out of the map book, 65 ter 9223. It's map 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Colonel Tucker, do you recognise the image on the screen?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, this is the map which -- or looks very similar to the map which Karadzic and General Mladic and Koljevic showed to General Morillon at one of our first meetings in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And when you were shown this map, you were describing before that there was a claim to any territory that was 50 per cent Serb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct. And on this map was drawn a line which bounded what Karadzic and General Mladic claimed was their land and was land of the self-proclaimed, self-styled Republika Srpska. And their logic was that if the land was more than 50 per cent populated by Serbs, then it was their land, and they were going to push out and had pushed out those who were not Serb out of those territories. And if the land was less than 50 per cent Serb, then they had no claim or made no claim upon that land. And the inference of what they were saying was that this line that they were -- had drawn on the map was what was effectively the frontline of the fighting between the -- primarily between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Colonel, as this is quite a colourful map, can you please describe or point out which aspects that Karadzic was claiming were going to be Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It's largely the blue areas, if I understand this map correctly, which are the over 50 per cent Bosnian Serb areas, and the frontline that they drew in order to describe the boundaries of their self-styled Republika Srpska basically adhered to the frontline as we United Nations understood it to be at that time. There were a couple of areas which were -- where their logic broke down because up in the north towards Brcko there was a very narrow piece of Bosnian Serb land with the Drina River on the north and the Bosnian Muslims on the south, and that was of strategic importance to them in order to link Western Serb territory with the Eastern Serb territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again, if we could have a date of this meeting, that would be of some help.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I believe it was given before, but I'll re-ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell me when you had these meetings in Pale?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: This meeting, I believe, was at the beginning of November 1992. We had actually first met with General Mladic and Karadzic in Lukavica on the outskirts of Sarajevo, but that was just before Karadzic going to Geneva. And it was just before General Mladic's last attempt to seize Sarajevo or at least cut Sarajevo in half, which was the 36-hour offensive which was carried out around 29, 30 November -- 30 October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, your answers have provided two additional lines of questioning. First, you indicated that the Serbs intended to push out non-Serbs in the blue areas. How did they --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, that's a misstatement. That would be the Bosnian Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, how did the Bosnian Serbs intend to push out the non-Bosnian Serb population?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We know as United Nations from military fact that people were rounded up out of their houses, put into trucks, carted off, put in --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that the Court does not approve of objecting to an answer, but the question was quite specific and I would ask Ms. Carter to direct the witness to answer the question. The question was a question of intent and how did the Bosnian Serbs intend to do something. The answer responds by not only hearsay, unattributed hearsay, "we know from the United Nations" which is a relatively vague answer. This dealt with a meeting that he was having with two specific people and to the extent in that meeting they exhibited their intent, he can respond in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Can you please answer. There's an objection, Madam Carter, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I'm happy to rephrase the question if it pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not the question that is being objected to, it is the answer that is not answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please answer the question as you were asked. How did Karadzic say he was going to accomplish the push-out of the non-Bosnian Serb population?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: He didn't go into details.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were you aware at that time of how the push-out of the non-Bosnian Serb population was occurring?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, because I was in the chain of command of the UN military forces in Bosnia, and our soldiers were reporting what they had seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What were they reporting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: They were reporting that people were being rounded up or had been rounded up out of their houses, houses had been put on fire, and people had been taken away and then transported to frontlines and then released. There were moves inside Sarajevo where people were being put on buses and being transported out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: For the record, I would once again -- I would object to any unsourced hearsay being elicited. If the gentleman can source the hearsay, that would be fine. But otherwise, it is irrelevant and of not much use to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is unsourced hearsay?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "Our soldiers were reporting" who, what, when, where, how? How can you rely on that information? It's information that has no basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Especially when you are dealing with it from the stand point of the military as we know. Within the military there would be -- if such reports are being made, then such documents would be available to the gentleman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've understood your objection. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the very beginning of the response indicated that he was in the chain of command of the UN forces and those were the soldiers that he was receiving the reports from. He directly sourced the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know which specific soldiers he sourced them from within the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please describe the chain of command in the BH forces, UNPROFOR forces?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The main reporting that I saw in the chain of command was daily reports which were produced by each of the battalions in UN BH commands. These were compiled and sent every night from the respective battalions to the headquarters of UN BH command. And one of my responsibilities was to read those reports every morning because they came in overnight, and General Morillon and I would then discuss them first thing in the morning, and that was a daily routine.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you describe the reporting of what was occurring to the non-Serb population, is this the same structure that you received that information?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The reporting structure that you just set out, is that how you were learning about the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Partially. There was also the -- what I would refer to as the the "Jajce incident" which happened at the end of October, which is when the Bosnian Serb forces attacked, seized, and captured the town of Jajce. Reports from the British battalion in whose area that was taking place said that Jajce had become a collecting area for many refugees who had been ejected from Bosnian Serb territory. And the town was then -- which was full of refugees was then attacked by the Bosnian Serbs and a long column of refugees was then fleeing from Jajce towards Travnik. And there were reports from the British battalion which had soldiers in positions watching this retreat of refugees and the column of refugees was reported by the British as being shelled with artillery from Bosnian Serb forces to their north. And because this was a live event, this was not reported in the 24 hourly report that I was describing because this was live action. This was being reported throughout the days in the end of -- towards the end of October. That was one particular event by which I formed the knowledge that I described earlier. The second was that in Sarajevo around the end of October, beginning of November, there were a large number of Croats who were being bused, I believe Serbs as well, though I can't remember exactly, who were being bused out of Sarajevo down towards -- down in the direction of Split. I can't remember the exact routing anymore. But that was the second event which was taking place at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned the Jajce incident. How long was the refugee column?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: There were reports that the refugee column was about 30 kilometres long.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Moving back to the meeting at Pale, what did Karadzic and Mladic tell you about the people -- the Muslim areas that were going to be a part of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: They did not talk specifically about Muslim areas that were going to be a part. They simply said that this, as the map that they were showing me with a line on it, was what they claimed was Republika Srpska, that they claimed international recognition of Republika Srpska, that they were an independent country, an independent nation, and that they did not want to have anything to do with the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, the reporting that you heard about the pushing out of the Muslim population, how long had that been going on?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I only arrived in Bosnia towards the end of October 1992. I had only seen newspaper reporting prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And how long was it being reported that the Muslim population was being pushed out?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: From newspaper reports, it would appear that that had started in late April, early May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What media outlets were covering Bosnia at that time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: In other words, May to the time before I deployed to Bosnia I was reading UK, US newspapers and was seeing UK, US, and CNN television broadcasting news outlets.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would call up P -- I'm sorry, if I can submit 65 ter 9223 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 9223 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit P2693. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would now like to bring up Exhibit P2440 at page 2, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when specifically did you arrive in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought he just answered the question a little earlier. He said October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm looking for a date, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A date. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me what day you arrived in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I believe it was about the 26th, 25th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If we can move to page 2, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is the report of the Special Rapporteur of the Commission on Human Rights, a Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki who toured Bosnia from 12 to 22 October 1992. What he found was that human rights violations were being continued and that a great number of people have lost their lives and thousands more find their dignity violated. Furthermore, Mr. Mazowiecki found the Muslim population are the principal victims. Based on your experiences in October of 1992, do you agree with Mr. Mazowiecki's reporting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I now move to page 3 of the same report, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mr. Mazowiecki also came to the view that the principal objective of the military conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina is the establishment of ethnically homogenous regions and that ethnic cleansing does not appear to be the consequence of the war, but rather the goal. Based on your experiences, do you share Mr. Mazowiecki's view?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, without further establishment of some form of, at this point, expertise, that view, although I'm sure is a sincere one and firmly held by Colonel Tucker, is personal and irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that Mr. Tucker is here as an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Am I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Or that he should have -- he should be coming as an expert witness to be able to give that view?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Certainly to be able to give that kind of a view. Absolutely. These are clearly ultimate facts upon which this Chamber is going to have to decide. His personal experiences may well have brought him to a particular conclusion, and with regard to his personal conclusion, I would not have an argument with the gentleman. But further than that, I don't think that such opinions have any relevance. And as a matter of fact, in this regard, they are highly prejudicial, and I would submit that any -- that the prejudice outweighs the probative value in all respects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is basing this opinion on his personal knowledge and his conversations with the principals who were a part of this plan. He described on the map that Karadzic showed him that that is precisely what they were doing. So I am merely tying Mr. Mazowiecki's report to the evidence that the witness has just previously stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is the problem that we are now encountering this objection because it doesn't seem apparent that you -- what you asked this witness's opinion is based on what he himself saw and observed and heard from the participants, but what he sees from this report. I'm sure he can give you that opinion without this exhibit on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I merely showed the witness the exhibit because the Court's previous ruling with regards to this exhibit was that it was going to notice rather than the truth of the contents therein. So we -- in order to follow along with the Court's ruling, I'm attempting to show it to the witness to put it in some realtime context.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think they are -- I also think they are doing something else, which is self-evident from what she just said, which is now they are attempting to establish the truth of the contents therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which is -- this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which has already been ruled upon to their detriment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, this is an exhibit, that's why she's not trying to confirm it. In that event, then I think you should proceed and the objection would be overruled. If that is the purpose of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, following up on the Court's comments, the information that you see before you, you said you share Mr. Mazowiecki's views. Can you tell me specifically what did you learn while on the ground in Bosnia that leads you to these opinions?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The first thing is the meeting in Pale with the census map that I've just described to you. The second was the military assessment that we in UN Bosnia-Herzegovina command made, which was that by the end of October, early November 1992, that the Bosnian Serbs had achieved their military objectives. In other words, they had achieved the seizure of the land that Karadzic had described. What they wanted thereafter was recognition of the status quo that they had seized. Their objective in all the negotiations with United Nations was a cease-fire across the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina along all of the frontlines. What they objected to was the Bosnian Muslims who would continue to attack in one place and then another, and then when the Bosnian Serbs counter-attacked, then the Bosnian Muslims would plead for the United Nations forces to broker a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, moving back to the initial question, you indicated that the reason you formed this opinion about the ethnic cleansing was based on your meeting with Karadzic as well as the information you were receiving from your troops. Did anything else lead to your opinion in regards to the campaign of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We were still receiving newspaper reports. We had press people who every day looked at newspaper reporting and then produced summaries of extracts of the main news events, which were relevant to us in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when you met with Karadzic - and I no longer need the exhibit - when you met with Karadzic in November 1992, what was UNPROFOR's position with regards to the plan?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: UNPROFOR's position, which General Morillon emphasised, was to facilitate the supply of humanitarian aid to all people in need, regardless of their ethnic backgrounds. In order to -- one of the main reasons, one of the main obstacles to the provision of humanitarian aid was fighting, and so General Morillon offered the good offices of his UNPROFOR personnel in order to assist the brokering of cease-fires wherever there was fighting going on in order to facilitate the passage of humanitarian supply convoys, relief convoys.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient point?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at quarter to. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Colonel Tucker, you were describing the conflict in Sarajevo, or you mentioned the conflict in Sarajevo. Can you please tell me, what were the tactics that the Bosnian Serb army was using inside of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb army was not in Sarajevo. It was surrounding Sarajevo. The -- as I described earlier, the Bosnian Serb objective was recognition of the status quo that they had achieved. However, the Bosnian Muslims did not accept that and so the Bosnian Muslims --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again I would ask Ms. Carter to control the witness. The question was very specific, "What were the tactics the Bosnian Serb army was using inside of Sarajevo." And I believe he has answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell me what military tactics was the Bosnian Serb army employing with regards to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: There was -- there were two tactics. One was to reply with overwhelming force using heavy weapons, to respond to any Bosnian Muslim attacks out of Sarajevo. The second was to randomly shell Sarajevo in what -- and this is my interpretation as a military observer, terrorism by artillery, by indirect fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please describe what you are talking about, what was going on with the shelling?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: There would be fairly continuous shelling throughout the day and night, sometimes more intensively, sometimes less intensively, but there was not aimed at any particular military objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How were the civilians being impacted by this tactic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It caused uncertainty and nobody knew where the next shells would fall. And often civilians were injured or killed by these shells, so they were under -- in a state of constant fear of where would the next shells fall.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you give a specific example where the Bosnian Serb army replied with overwhelming force using heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, that question is leading. And second of all, it's vague, meaning specific example in terms of date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, the question leads from page 34 starting at line 11 where he describes the two tactics. And one was to reply with overwhelming force using heavy weapons. I'm just trying to follow up on the previous response by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you give an example of this overwhelming force?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: One example is when in early December 1992 the Muslims -- the Bosnian Muslims attacked out of the Stup area, which is a suburb at the western end of Sarajevo. The Bosnian Muslims caught the Bosnian Serbs initially by surprise. The initial response from the Bosnian Serbs was to concentrate as much artillery fire as they could. Several days later, they had managed to bring some reinforcements of their very limited regular infantry and armour, armoured vehicles to the area and then counter-attacked, and then recaptured the territory of which the Bosnian Muslims had temporarily captured. And they then, the Bosnian Serbs, then proceeded to shell very heavily the suburbs of Sarajevo from which the Bosnian Muslim attacks had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Well, if they were shelling the place where the attacks had taken place, how was that inappropriate or overwhelming force?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Because they shelled not just the direct location of where the attacks had taken place, but they shelled the suburbs behind there in what I would describe as punishment attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How many shells were falling on those suburbs?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Many hundreds per day.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And how long did this attack occur?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: This particular attack around Stup went on -- the initial Muslim attack was around a day, a day and a half, maybe two days long. The Bosnian Serb counterattacks then took another week and then petered out over a further week.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You also described the random shelling of Sarajevo which you called, but is not charged in this case, terrorism by artillery or by indirect fire. Can you please give an example of that tactic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Objection. Not only relevance, but also with regard to the issue of terrorism, that's a matter that has been discussed on innumerable occasions. It's something that, I believe, the Prosecution has agreed would not be led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- the as I pointed out that is not charged, what I'm trying to determine is what he was referring to in the randomly shelling of Sarajevo. And I was just putting it in his response, he gave that answer. I'm merely trying in order not to lead or rephrase the witness's question using his own words.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate what Ms. Carter has said, but with regard to the issue of terror or terrorism, the Prosecution is well aware of the concerns and this is something that we have agreed upon during the pendency of this trial, and I believe we are trying to get into the back door with what we've agreed won't come in through the front door. It's inappropriate to be using that language at this time. Whether or not the witness has used those words, it is inappropriate to lead in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just asked my fellow Judges to confirm, it does seem as if the Chamber is not aware of this agreement, and I don't know whether -- is this an agreement between the parties from which the Chamber was excluded or is this an agreement that the Chamber is supposed to be privy to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well it comes from -- it comes from -- it actually stems from a ruling that was made by the Chamber in May of 2007 with regard to the application of the Rule 73(B) amendment of the indictment, I believe it's paragraph 16 of that particular ruling. With regard to the agreement, I think it would be fair to say that it has not been a formal agreement. However, every time this issue has come up, and there has been issues about what particular evidence would be led by specific witnesses and the issue of terror has been raised, it has been agreed that it would not be led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the question -- my question was, is this an agreement between the parties or is it an agreement to which the Chamber is supposed to be privy?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that it is a combination of an understanding of the decision that was made by this Chamber with regard to the the Rule 73 amendment of the indictment made in May of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you quote the ruling, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure, the Chamber notes paragraph 16, May 2007. "The Chamber notes that at least 22 witnesses are scheduled to give evidence on terror in Sarajevo. Two of the 22 witnesses are scheduled to give evidence on the 'terror count.' As the amended indictment does not include a terror count, the relevance of this type of testimony is not apparent. Although the Prosecution alleges a 'protracted campaign of sniping and shelling upon Sarajevo,' there is no indication in the amended indictment that a protracted campaign is being alleged in support of charge of Terror against the accused. Only one indication on terror is given in the pre-trial brief: The Prosecution asserts that written" -- italicised -- "evidence will be presented in support of the assumption that inter alia, the nature or purpose of the aforementioned campaign was to spread terror amongst the Serbian population of Sarajevo. However, this does not justify the presentation of extensive evidence on this aspect of the campaign. Therefore, the Trial Chamber will instruct the Prosecution not to lead evidence on 'terror' in relation to the Sarajevo count." Now, I understand that this is not evidence which is charged in the indictment, however, it seems to be inappropriate to be leading such evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, I just ask you to quote that for us. Madam Carter, it seems that there is a ruling here by Chamber that evidence on terror shall not be led.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the evidence that I'm attempting to lead is specifically the random shelling of Sarajevo. That was described as one ever the tactics. I am a just trying to lead evidence about is there a specific example of that tactic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is allowed. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that the second tactic used by the Bosnian Serb army was to randomly shell Sarajevo. Can you please give a specific example of that tactic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: There was one event that I can describe which was on the night of Christmas Eve 1992 when on the stroke of midnight every Bosnian Serb gun, artillery piece, mortar, anti-aircraft gun surrounding Sarajevo opened fire into Sarajevo firing as fast as they could for a period of about 15 or 20 minutes. There was a 40 millimetre anti-aircraft gun mounted on the hill-side above the Presidency, above the residency in Sarajevo which is where General Morillon's headquarters inside Sarajevo was, and which is where I was located at the time of this incident. And this artillery gun is a rapid-fire anti-aircraft gun and fired a cadence of boom-boom boom-boom-boom boom-boom, boom-boom boom-boom-boom boom-boom, for about 15 minutes firing into the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: 15 minutes. Not five zero.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, unfortunately for the record we won't be able to get the specific boom booms that you gave out. Are you indicating that there was a repeated pattern to the shelling?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Of that particular gun, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Is it possible that that's simply how that gun-fires?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Because it's an anti-aircraft gun and it would normally fire a burst which would be four, five, six, maybe ten shells in rapid fire one after the other. The gun has a trigger and the gunner of that particular gun was clearly pressing that trigger specifically in order to fire out that particular pattern, cadence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, you described that these tactics caused uncertainty in the civilian population of Sarajevo. How was this uncertainty portrayed within the city?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: People were very afraid, people were very anxious, people did not like going outside into the open. And particularly into open areas, they would run across open areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, what were the living conditions like for the people inside of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The living conditions inside Sarajevo worsened during the winter and the cold and were appalling. There was no heating. There was virtually no gas coming into Sarajevo. There was virtually no electricity coming into Sarajevo, so there was no heating. Temperatures were down to minus 10, minus 15 degrees centigrade at times during the winter and every single piece of wood in the city was stripped out and every single tree and the roots were dug out of the ground in order to burn. There was very little water, and sanitation was very difficult, and people were very hungry, and you could see that there were no fat people in Sarajevo. Everybody was thin. People were permanently hungry.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, was there any outsiders reporting about the events in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: There were international media present inside Sarajevo and in particular they tended to stay in, I believe, it was the Holiday Inn which was a predominant hotel in the middle of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Which media outlets were covering the siege of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: There were a number of independent journalists. There were also journalists who were tied to the BBC, to CNN, to Agence France-Presse, and to US newspapers who would come into, at least Sarajevo, for a week, two weeks, and would then seek interviews with General Morillon and others and would then report and then leave, come back six weeks later or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were any local or Balkan media outlets covering the siege of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Inside Sarajevo there was "Oslobodenje" which was a Bosnian Muslim newspaper which continued to print even during -- even throughout the siege.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd now like to move your testimony to the east and Srebrenica. Can you please tell me, when did the eastern enclaves first come to your attention in your role as an UNPROFOR officer?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The eastern enclaves came to my personal attention the first day that we arrived in Bosnia. I was already aware of their existence because of international newspaper reporting of attempts under the previous commander of Sector Sarajevo, General MacKenzie, who had tried to get humanitarian aid convoys into Gorazde escorted by Ukrainian, by soldiers from the Ukrainian battalion based in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why were humanitarian aid convoys necessary in the eastern enclaves?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The eastern enclaves had been surrounded and isolated by the initial Bosnian Serb attacks in May, June 1992, and when the Bosnian Serb military had seized the land that I described earlier that General Mladic and Karadzic showed me on the census map, they had seized those and surrounded those areas, as I said, in May or June, but had not done much more than isolate them. They were in quite mountainous terrain which was of little economic interest to the Bosnian Serbs who seemed to just leave them be, but isolate them and --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, let me stop you right there. You are using the words "isolation of the eastern enclaves," and the initial question was: Why were the humanitarian aid convoys necessary in the eastern enclaves. What was the ground-level reality for the people inside those enclaves?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Those enclaves were surrounded by Bosnian Serb forces who prevented food, any kind of supply, getting into those enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you please tell the Court what areas are considered the "eastern enclaves"?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The eastern enclaves were mainly centred around the town of Gorazde, around the town of Zepa, and around the town of Srebrenica, and around the village of Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that in May or June these areas were surrounded and that the Ukrainians had tried to provide humanitarian aid at some point. Do you know when specifically the Ukrainian battalion attempted aid to these enclaves?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The dates before I arrived in Bosnia I do not know other than I can recollect reading newspaper articles. In the time -- from the time that I arrived in Bosnia, the Ukrainian battalion made a number of attempts, and again by -- from memory it would be about three or four attempts to get to Srebrenica and about two attempts to get to Gorazde. The -- they did manage to get a convoy into Srebrenica at the beginning of December 1992, and that was the first humanitarian aid convoy that reached Srebrenica since the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What prevented these humanitarian aid convoys from getting into the region?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb forces and authorities put roadblocks on the road and prevented these convoys from proceeding and kept on coming up with different reasons as to why they would not be allowed to proceed from this roadblock further up the road, and eventually six hours later permission would come and then they would go and they would be stopped 3 kilometres further, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you bring this prevention to the attention of anybody?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. We -- this was one of the permanent subjects of General Morillon's discussions every time he met with any of the Bosnian Serb military or political people.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How often did this subject come up?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: At every meeting. And these meetings were taking place with the Bosnian Serbs almost daily.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What excuses were given as to why the convoys could not pass?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: One excuse was that the Bosnian Serbs demanded to search the convoys to make sure that there were no weapons hidden in amongst the -- the humanitarian aid, the food and the medicines, et cetera. When they insisted on doing that, it meant that the food was all ripped apart and that the food was spoiled. They also used the excuse that there was fighting on the road up ahead and that they could not guarantee the safety of the convoy and that they were not allowed to pass. Another excuse was that the locals living in the village, town, or whatever had had suffered many losses and were up in arms and were protesting about this convoy being allowed through and were blocking the road and were not allowing the convoy to pass through. Another excuse was to claim that they would allow convoys through to Bosnian Muslim areas only when similar convoys were sent to Bosnian Serb refugee areas as well. And they claimed that there was an imbalance in the amount of aid that was being provided to the refugees of the different ethnic backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were these excuses acceptable to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Relevance.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when you met with the Bosnian Serb political and military leaders and these excuses were given, how did UNPROFOR react?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm tempted to ask whether or not Ms. Carter believes that the gentleman has a mouse in his pocket. He can testify as to how he reacted and what he said or he can testify as regards to what he heard some other specific individual said, but to ask the question how UNPROFOR reacted is a bit problematic because UNPROFOR, as we learned from this witness, is a relatively large organisation that as I understand it has its headquarters in Zagreb. So I don't know whether or not as the question is presently framed Ms. Carter is suggesting that when there was a conversation between anyone in which Colonel Tucker was present that Zagreb was involved or whether or not we are speaking about specific individuals. I would once again ask as I've asked before that we have some specificity here because among other things we are referring to specific conversations with regard to specific subject matters on specific dates that will ultimately have an impact not only with regard to the cross-examination, but also with regard to the kinds of factual determines that the Chamber is going to have to make. And to ask this kind of a vague question is not helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm indicating that the conversations are the ones that Colonel Tucker was in fact present at. I believe that that is specific. However, I can be even more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when you and General Morillon spoke with Bosnian Serb political and military personnel and you received these excuses, what was your response?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: General Morillon --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, first of all, that assumes that within each -- that in the context of each of the meetings they received the same excuses. And the reason I'm pressing the point for specificity is, as Ms. Carter appreciates, this is a highly fluid time during the period in which many many things were occurring. So to ask broad-based questions with regard to how specific -- with regard to what specific people said and what was specifically done in regard to what was said is not helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, are you able to elicit from the witness specific responses to specific excuses that were given. Maybe take them one by one.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
