utterances.text: Sir, when is the first time you brought the humanitarian aid convoys to the attention of, we'll start with the Serb military, with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: In order to answer a question like that referring to events 15 years ago or more, I would need to refer to specific meetings. What I can say here now is that it was a subject in the first meetings that we had at the end of October, early November, and continued to be a subject of meetings throughout my time in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I presume we are talking of October, November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated that it came up at your first meeting. At your first meeting, what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The need to allow humanitarian aid through to all those in need regardless of which ethnic background that they came from. And that -- and General Morillon pressed the point that it was the responsibility of all in the region whether they were Serb, Muslim, or Croats, to help the United Nations forces move humanitarian aid to where it was needed. General Morillon also made the point, and there were a number of meetings where Jose Maria Mendiluce from UNHCR was involved. And who --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We've now -- once again I would ask Ms. Carter to control her witness. We are talking about the first meeting. We are not talking about anything but the first meeting. If the question is about subsequent meetings, then he can respond to those questions. I really must press the point here, Your Honour, and it will become evident through the fullness of time why this is of importance. The question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe. Okay. Fine. You can cut out that last sentence where the witness is saying that General Morillon also made the point and there were a number of meetings. Can you deal with one meeting at a time, please, Mr. Tucker. You were talking about the first meeting that you had in October, November 1992. Are you able to tell us about that, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you first provide a date. What day did you first meet on the subject?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I believe it was about the 27th or the 28th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. When is the second meeting that you discussed this?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It would have been in early -- around the 5th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The first meeting with General Mladic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You got to make sure, Madam Carter, that you are on a wave length with the witness. You've asked him about the second meeting and you followed up by saying who was present at that meeting, the answer is the first meeting. You were on the second meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell me -- well, we'll flesh out what you were just saying. Can you tell me who was present at the first meeting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: There were a number of people present at the first meeting. The ones who I particularly recall were General Mladic, Dr. Karadzic, Professor Koljevic, General Morillon, myself, and Adjutant Chief Mihailov who was General Morillon's body-guard. There were other people as well but I cannot, here, 15 years later, recall all their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And as to the second meeting, who was present there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The second meeting was Karadzic, Mladic, I believe Gvero was there, and again General Morillon, myself, and Mihailov. There were others there as well. Typically there were about eight or ten people in total at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In relation to that second meeting, what did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: There were many things that we discussed. One of them was the humanitarian aids to the eastern enclaves, but there was also the issue of the deployment of the Canadian battalion into the Banja Luka area. There was the deployment of the French battalion around Petrovac. There was permission for engineers to go into the no-man's land between -- surrounding Sarajevo in order to repair gas and electricity and water facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, focusing on the humanitarian aid, what was said about why the -- excuse me. From BH command's position, what was your concern at the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We repeated that humanitarian aid was being dispensed equitably, and it was driven by the independently assessed need on the the ground as opposed to a 50/50, and that General Morillon expected that the Bosnian Serb authorities to do everything in their power to ensure that this aid got through.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What was the Bosnian Serb response?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: General Morillon -- General Mladic and Karadzic said they would do everything that they could, but that it was not easy because there were strong emotions on the ground and sometimes locals did not do what they were told to do. They also asked for General Morillon to provide a proposed route so that General Mladic's staff could verify its or suggest alternatives so that the convoy would be able to reach its objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that there were "strong emotions on the ground." Are you aware or were you advised what those emotions were?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I cannot recall if at that specific meeting we were told, but it was always the same, which is that locals had suffered badly in the conflict and were objecting to aid passing through to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said that was during the first week of November. When was the third meeting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It was later in November. I can't remember the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At the time of the third meeting, had humanitarian aid gotten through to the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. There was -- at the third meeting, the convoy was underway and Mladic kept leaving the the room in order to go and speak on the telephone with his people in order to -- or this is what he was telling us, in order to try and make sure that the convoy got through.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Between the second and the third meeting, how much time had passed?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: A couple of weeks. This is meetings with General Mladic. There were many other meetings as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What were the other meetings?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The other meetings were with the Bosnian Muslims. At that stage, General Morillon did not have any meetings with the the Bosnian Croats. I think he met Colonel Siber for the first time in November.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When did the first convoy actually get through, and to which enclave did it reach?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I believe that a convoy reached Gorazde sometime in October/November, but the first convoy to reach Srebrenica was in -- at the beginning of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, can we just clarify. I thought you said that the second meeting was around the 5th of November. Now, and I thought you said that by that time of that meeting no convoy had gone through yet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No convoy had gone through to Srebrenica. My focus was on Srebrenica. The convoys to Gorazde were being driven by Sector Sarajevo of whom the Ukrainian battalion was a part. And I can't remember whether it was before the 5th of November or after the 5th of November that that convoy got through Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In regards to the eastern enclaves, and specifically with regards to Srebrenica, are you aware of how many people were inside of the Srebrenica enclave in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No, we were not. The United Nations did not have any of its own personnel in the enclaves and the only reports that were available were those from international news outlets who occasionally managed to get reporters into those areas. That's the only information that we had at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were you aware that the people in the enclaves were originally from those individual villages, or were they coming from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether my initial information was from reading those original news outlets, but what we subsequently, when we got our own people into the enclaves, found out was that there were many refugees in those enclaves who had fled there from other parts of Bosnia and who had been driven out of where they had previously lived by Bosnian Serb military, paramilitary, and police.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. When you say they were "driven out," are you aware of what tactics were being used to drive these people out of their villages?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The reports that these people -- or what these people told our soldiers when they were in the enclaves is that typically soldiers or people in military uniform or police uniform would come banging on their doors and tell them they had five minutes or whatever to assemble in the square or whatever, and that they were then put on to vehicles with whatever they could carry, and were then taken to a frontline, and were then told to get out of the vehicles and then walk in a particular direction. That was one approach. The other approach was that people would hear that this was happening in next village or the next suburb and they would not wait until people came knocking on the door, and they themselves just picked up what they could carry and of their own volition as it were would just leave and try to find safety somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated that these people were reporting to the troops. Did they indicate why they would leave when they would hear about the pushes from the next village?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Because they believed --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm going to object to that question. There are a myriad reasons why. This is during a war. The question is absolutely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll repeat my question. You indicated that these people were reporting to the troops that they were leaving because of the pushes from the next village. Did they explain to you why they would do that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Because they believed their lives were at risk.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: From whoever was carrying out the, I'll use the word advisedly, the ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How long had this ethnic cleansing been going on?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I can say that it was going on whilst I was in Bosnia. I believe, from reading international media and television that it had been going on in Bosnia since the beginning of the conflict since April, May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. At any point in time were you able to enter the enclaves, or specifically Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I entered the Srebrenica enclave twice. In fact, about six or seven times, but the first time was not Srebrenica itself, it was Konjevic Polje which is about 15 or 20 kilometres to the north-west of Srebrenica. And that was on the 5th and 6th of March, 1992. I then, with General Morillon, went into the Srebrenica enclave again about the 10th, 11th of March, 1992, and that was into Srebrenica itself. And we were then in Srebrenica for the next two and a half to three weeks, albeit we left Srebrenica, the enclave that is, on a number of occasions to go and negotiate with Bosnian Serb military and authorities and then returned back into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you gave the dates in March of 1992, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Sorry, 1993, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If you were expressing concern about the humanitarian situation in October and November of 1992, what took so long for you to go to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The main reason was that we were working to priorities and in October we knew about the enclaves but we had very little information about the circumstances inside the enclaves, and there were other events taking place which seemed more acute and, therefore, we focused on those. The situation in the enclaves started escalating - and by escalating what I mean is that the Bosnian Muslim authorities in Sarajevo started increasingly demanding that United Nations and the international community do more in order to get humanitarian aid into the enclaves. And this started around middle of December 1992. And it then steadily increased in -- or rather, the Bosnian Muslim pressure on United Nations -- on General Morillon steadily increased throughout January, and that led to the setting up of airdrops of humanitarian aid into the enclaves because the United Nations was not succeeding in getting humanitarian -- land-based humanitarian convoys through. And then in February 1993 we heard reports about a lot more fighting going -- starting up again around the enclaves, and the Bosnian Muslim authorities were no longer only asking for humanitarian aid, but were also -- also started asking for aid for injured -- people injured in fighting. In other words, up until December/January, the enclaves were simply surrounded and isolated, whereas in January/February, fighting started building up and escalating around the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you had indicated that there were airdrops and other calls for humanitarian aid in the enclaves at the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993. Who were you and General Morillon speaking with in order to facilitate aid to the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Everybody and anybody who General Morillon was able to meet with. What I mean by that is that General Mladic refused to see General Morillon anymore, and the last meeting that he had with General Mladic was, I think, at the end of December, like the 26th of December. Then he didn't meet Mladic again for -- I think the next time he met Mladic was in Belgrade in March, at the end of March 1993. So in between he was having to meet with Karadzic, with General Gvero, I think he was a colonel at the time. There was a Colonel Zarkovic. . He met several times with General Milovanovic, who is the Chief of Staff, who is General Mladic's Chief of Staff. He also met a number of times with General Galic who was the commander of the Serb force -- Bosnian Serb forces surrounding Sarajevo. And he met in January/February with a number of Bosnian Serb politicians, members of the, I think they called it the assembly or the National Assembly of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you before this line disappears from the screen. Mr. Tucker, you said at page 54, starting from line 16 you said: "Then in February 1993 we heard reports about a lot more fighting going on starting up again around the enclaves, and the Bosnian Muslim authorities were no longer only asking for humanitarian aid, but were also started asking for aid for injured people, injured in fighting." In the notion of the United Nations, BH, what is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: BH command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Command. Was help to the injured not seen as humanitarian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just that I wanted -- thank you so much. Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you noted in your recitation with regards to Mladic, that at some point in time you met him in Belgrade at the end of 1993. Was that your only meeting with persons inside of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No, we met in, as I mentioned earlier this morning, with the Serb -- Serb Army high command in Belgrade in January 1993, and then we met at the end of March 1993 with Milosevic in Belgrade. And the day after or the day after that we met in Belgrade with General Mladic, Gvero, and about ten other military and political people from the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, and perhaps I'm confused here, I do apologise. With regard to the question that Ms. Carter has asked, it has as a reference point that he met with Mladic at the end of 1993 in Belgrade. It's my understanding that Colonel Tucker was no longer in the region at the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the end of March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So that's clear. Just because as the question reads it says -- because it's dealing with a series of meetings, I have some concern that as the question is presently put there would be the impression left that Colonel Tucker met with General Mladic in Belgrade at the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, just to make sure we don't have our wires crossed in regards to dates, when is the first time you met in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: In January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Who did you meet?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: General Panic and a number of senior officers from the Serb -- Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We requested -- General Morillon requested their assistance in exercising influence over their Bosnian Serb brethren to restrain themselves and to allow humanitarian aid through and to prevent military excesses from taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What was the response?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The response was that they would, of course, do everything in their power. However, they made the point that the Bosnian Serbs were an independent country and that whilst they could appeal to them, they had no authority over them, and had no -- had no power to direct them to act in any particular way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I am now going to take up the chronology of your entrance into Srebrenica and we'll discuss the later Belgrade meetings in a while. What specifically were the circumstances where you entered Srebrenica or near Srebrenica for the first time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The circumstances were that General Morillon had been increasingly urgently requested by the Muslim authorities in Sarajevo to go to Srebrenica to see for himself the situation on the ground, and to see for himself how urgent the situation was, and to make sure that humanitarian aid was no longer held up and blocked and would be made to get through to the besieged people in the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you describe your first entrance?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The first entrance into the Srebrenica pocket was 5th, 6th of March, 1993. And after eventually being allowed by the Bosnian Serbs to go into the enclave, we found in Konjevic Polje that there were not as many injured as had been reported to General Morillon by the authorities in Sarajevo, but that the majority of the walking wounded in the refugees had passed through Konjevic Polje and had moved on to Srebrenica. The next day, General Morillon went up to the village of Cerska. To do so he had to again cross the frontline because the village of Cerska had been captured by the -- by Bosnian Serb forces several days previously. And the refugees that I mentioned a couple of minutes ago, and the injured, were the ones who had come in the last few days from Cerska and who had escaped from Cerska before it was seized by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That was your first entrance into the Srebrenica pocket. Can you tell me when the second time was?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The second entrance into the Srebrenica pocket was about five days later, four days later. And because General Morillon having gone into Konjevic Polje and Cerska, went back to Sarajevo to meet with President Izetbegovic to tell him personally what he had seen, and President Izetbegovic then asked him, and Morillon suggested to him that it seemed as if Srebrenica was actually the place where the majority of the refugees were. So General Morillon said, I will now go back to Srebrenica itself. It then took about two or three more days before General Morillon managed to get into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why did it take two to three days?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Because he was stopped every 5 kilometres, every 10 kilometres, at roadblocks. And these -- at these roadblocks, you would be told that whoever was Manning the roadblock did not have authority to let General Morillon pass, so then there would be a wait of two, three, four hours. General Morillon would try to get on the telephone with people, and then eventually he would be allowed through and he would be stopped at the next roadblock and he would be accompanied by -- General Morillon would be accompanied by ten vehicles and then part of the permission to go through past the roadblock would that be that he left two vehicles behind, so then it would be eight vehicles and then at the next roadblock it would be six vehicles. We then eventually reached Zvornik and then we were told that the mayor of Zvornik had to approve General Morillon passing and so we then had to meet with the mayor of Zvornik, but he couldn't be found. So then we had to go and stay in the Hotel Yugoslavia which is just over the river in Serbia proper. We then met in the morning with the mayor of Zvornik who wanted General Morillon to approve a resupply of chemicals to a, I forget, something like an aluminium plant so that the plant could start working again and if General Morillon would do that, then they would allow General Morillon to ass. General Morillon protested against that linkage. Then a Major Pandurevic turned up and Major Pandurevic is a Bosnian Serb army officer who obviously had a lot of power and authority in that part of Bosnia, and Major Pandurevic then said that he would help and that he would give permission. Eventually we left the mayor of Zvornik's office and we were allowed to go to the bridge at Zvornik over the Drina River, and there the Bosnian Serb captain who commanded the bridge refused to let General Morillon cross. And so there was another stand-off for hours. Eventually he was given permission to cross over into Serbia and he was told he had to go on the road from Zvornik to Bratunac, but on the Serbian side of the river, not on the Bosnian side of the river. On the other side of the river were two or three UNHCR convoys trying to go the other direction, in other words, cross the bridge from Serbia into Bosnia, and they had been held up there for four or five days or longer. There was also the Canadian battalion, the 2nd Canadian battalion which was held up there and had been waiting there for three or four weeks just parked at the side of the road waiting for permission to deploy into Bosnia. We picked up an armoured personnel carrier from that Canadian battalion and took it with us because we only had jeeps, and one truck of supplies, of humanitarian aid of sugar and medicines, and we then eventually reached Bratunac where we had to meet with the local Bosnian Serb commander in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I don't mean to interrupt you, and you certainly have been responsive to what took so long, but also the answer has taken quite a long time as well and it appear that is that is the time for the break. If the Court would like to break now or we can finish the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How much more do you have to finish this answer, Mr. Tucker? Do you think you can wrap it up and we can break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In two minutes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, so we left this train in Bratunac, what happened once you reached there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Just before we got to Bratunac, we were again held up on the road between Zvornik and Bratunac for two or three hours. When we reached Bratunac, we were told that the bridge on the road from Bratunac to Srebrenica had been blown up the previous day and was now impassable, a bridge called the Yellow Bridge. And then I looked at the map and found a small hill road that went up through the hills and the mountains into Srebrenica and the Serbs said, Oh, we don't know about that. And so we said, Well, we'll try it. And they obviously had no orders to stop us from doing that. And so rather reluctantly lets go up that route and that's how we eventually, taking about eight or ten hours, managed to get into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when we left off just before the break, you were about to enter Srebrenica proper for the first time. Can you please describe what you saw on that first day?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We arrived in darkness, so it wasn't until a few hours later that we could actually begin to see, and we then walked around Srebrenica in order to see with our own eyes what the situation was. The temperature was well below zero. There was thick snow on the ground. There were thousands of refugees huddled in the streets and around buildings. There was a wasteland next to the PTT building where there were wrecked cars. These wrecked cars didn't have any engines or wheels, but each car had about eight people living in it. A couple in the engine compartment, a couple in the boot, and then four or five or six in the actual passenger compartment. We were taken to the school building in Srebrenica which was jam packed with people. You could barely walk anywhere without stepping on people. These people were very hungry, very cold. The smell in the place -- in any place where people were packed closely together in the cold was indescribable. It was a smell of rancid butter. The smell of human bodies who hadn't been washed in many -- in a long time. We were taken to blocks of flats where there were 15, 20 people to a room. The stairwells in these blocks of flats, these apartment buildings, the corridors, every space had people crouched desperately with blankets and coats, and whatever they could around them. People showed us what they were eating. They were eating little cakes made from a yellow flour which could be found on the hills surrounding Sarajevo. These people were, as I said, thin, obviously very hungry. Their eyes were dull. These people had no hope. They were listless. Basic hygiene wasn't being attended to. People were not supporting each other. It was an extraordinarily depressing sight, and it is one of the worst things that I have ever seen in my life.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, as you were walk around the streets of Srebrenica, did you have an opportunity to speak with anybody?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I personally did not directly speak with many people other than a couple of members of the Srebrenica war committee who happened to speak English. We had General Morillon's body-guard who was a Macedonian and spoke Serbo-Croat, he was a foreign legion soldier, and whenever we wanted to talk with people, General Morillon would ask through his body-guard, and it's through this body-guard in most cases that we interacted with local people through language.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you interact with the local people on that day?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What did you learn?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The people told us that they came from many areas, but most of them had the people who were either out in the open or in the school or in these apartment blocks had fled to Srebrenica within the last two, three, four weeks. And they had done so, and most of them came from villages which had been within the Srebrenica enclave, but the Bosnian Serbs had apparently started attacking again in early February and they had started shelling villages, and these people had fled from these villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when the villages were being shelled, was there any sort of pattern or plan to that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The pattern that we observed was that the Bosnian Serbs would start shelling two or three villages, and by shelling what I mean is one shell every 20 minutes, then a pause of an hour, then three more shells. So it wasn't a fierce Second World War style military bombardment, but it was just desultory dropping of shells on a village. When they first started, the villagers described not really knowing what this was about. However, after two or three days, then suddenly in a quick attack say 50 soldiers, 70 soldiers, infantry, a couple of tanks and a couple of armoured personnel carriers would then suddenly in a pincer movement attack a village and capture it. And then a couple of days later it was the next village, then the next village. And the refugees told us that they very quickly spotted the pattern that the shelling was a precursor to the ground attack which would follow in two or three days' time. So after the first few days when the fighting flared up around the Srebrenica enclave, all it took was for the Bosnian Serbs to start firing a few shells into a village for all the villager just to pick up the bags and flee. One of the tragedies was that in these villages in rural and mountainous areas, these villages had stalk piles and stores --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, let me stop you right there. So you are indicating these villages were falling in a pattern, but you also said what you observed. Now, were you observing this pattern or were you only hearing it from the villagers themselves?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We were hearing the pattern reported to us. The first time we came across this was when we were speaking with villagers on that first day in Srebrenica when we were walking around. Secondly, is when we went into Srebrenica, we had with us a number of UNMOs, who were unarmed UN observers. And after we arrived in Srebrenica, these UNMOs went out every day into the enclave with Bosnian Serb guides. And they went and their task was to go and see for themselves what was happening. And they then reported back to General Morillon and myself and confirmed that they were seeing this pattern as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who was participating in these shellings?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Where the shells came from, obviously we did not know, but the soldiers who then attacked on the ground were Bosnian Serb [sic] soldier, so the assumption has to be that the shells were fired by the Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And so just for clarification, at page 65, line 10, you indicated it was Bosnian Serb guides that were taking you around to the village --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Sorry, Bosnian Muslim guides inside the enclave who were taking the UNMOs to the frontline in order to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, I stopped you earlier when you started describing the plight of those who were pushed out of some of the smaller villages. Can you please tell us what made their situation unique?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Their situation was that in their homes they had stores of food, even though not much, they had something. When they fled, they could only flee with what they could carry or what their mule could carry. In other words, they had much less food with them. So these displaced refugees were the ones who were suffering the most from hunger and from cold.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You were describing a very packed village in Srebrenica. Did you have an approximation of how many people were present in that a village?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: There were various people who had various estimates. The talk was from different people, by different people. I mean, we had a couple of UNHCR people, we had a couple of WHO people. There were some people from Medicins Sans Frontieres and a estimate varied from 20.000 to 40.000 in and around Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Srebrenica on that first day or in that first period?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It was from about the 11th of March, 1993. And I finally left Srebrenica on about the 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. During your time in Srebrenica, did you only communicate with those inside the village, or did you communicate outside the village?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: headquarters in Kiseljak. We also had a US Army team with us who had come with us in order to coordinate airdrops of humanitarian aid. And they had a satellite radio with them called a TacSat which they used to speak with the United States European command in Frankfurt. This same radio was also able to speak with the United States aircraft carrier which was in the Adriatic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, outside of the communications that you had via phone calls and that type of thing with your command, did you have any communication with Serbian or Bosnian Serbian officials in regards to what you saw?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. We met -- General Morillon had a number of meetings with Bosnian Serbs. Initially with General Milovanovic, several meetings with General Milovanovic which took place at the Yellow Bridge, which is this bridge in between Bratunac and Srebrenica, which was over the river. And that river was at the time the front line between the Bosnian Serb and Bosnian Muslim forces in that area. General Morillon also later had meetings with people in Bratunac itself, the mayor of Bratunac, the local Bosnian Serb commander in Bratunac. He had meetings with Major Pandurevic on the outskirts of Zvornik. He also met Pandurevic and another colonel, whose name I can't remember, near the bridge at Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Let me stop there. When you met with Pandurevic, what did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The meeting with Pandurevic was mainly about letting General Morillon pass and letting humanitarian aid convoys through, because it seemed that Pandurevic had a lot of control over what happened in the area. Pandurevic -- General Morillon also requested Pandurevic to do everything he could to stop the UNHCR convoys which were being blocked in Zvornik, to stop them being blocked, and to allow them to go through.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Where specifically were you meeting with Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We met with Pandurevic a number of times. We met with him outside by the bridge -- first time we met Pandurevic was in the mayor of Zvornik's office on the way into Srebrenica. We then met with him near the the bridge at Bratunac. We met with him in what looked like his headquarters on the outskirts of Zvornik. It was a military barracks and we had been blocked and Pandurevic took us to his office in order --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Whilst he was "seeking permission for General Morillon to proceed."

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please describe his offices?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: His office was in a military installation, a barracks. And inside his office on the wall by his desk there were some military maps hanging on the wall, and this map had marked on it the -- was showing the area of the Srebrenica enclave, and this map showed a series of lines, and the biggest line around the outside had the date 7th of February on it. And then the next line, which was smaller, had the date of 10th of February, and there were about six or seven further lines, each line more recent with the last line being a couple of days previous. These lines looked as if they were describing the perimeter of the Srebrenica enclave, and they showed a steady progression of diminishing size of the enclave. When Pandurevic led Morillon and myself into this office, he just led us in and told us to sit down and he would get us a cup of coffee and walked out. When he came back in again, he realised that this map was showing on the wall and there was a curtain over it, and he went and pulled the curtain over the map so we couldn't see it anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: May we briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If I can have one brief moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when we left off on your testimony, you were describing the steady progression and diminishing size of the Srebrenica enclave as depicted on the map in Pandurevic's wall. Can you please advise the Court, was this map consistent with what you and the other units on the ground were seeing in and around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, this map showed in more detail than we had available from our sparse reporting, but where we did have information, this map was consistent. And as a trained military officer, that map seemed to indicate the progression of the Bosnian Serb assault onto the enclave of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Outside of your meetings with Pandurevic, you indicated that you also had meetings with other persons. Once you learned about this plan, who did you speak with?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The plan -- seeing this map did not tell us anything we didn't already know. We knew that fighting had started around the Srebrenica enclave -- heavy fighting had started towards the end of January, early February, and that the enclave was being steadily made smaller. And we spoke with -- or General Morillon spoke with Bosnian Serb leaders, I've already described meetings with General Milovanovic and others, at which he requested them to stop the attacks on the enclave pointing out that whilst they -- the Bosnian Muslims were very angry about the attacks which the Bosnian Muslims had started carrying out from --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you were actually asked who did you speak -- did you speak to anybody about the plan. Did you have any other meetings either with Bosnian Serb or Serbian officials with regards to this operation in and around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I think -- excuse me. I think at this point we are moving a bit far afield. The initial question stems from the following: "Sir, when the villages were being shelled was there any sort of pattern or plan to that?" And the gentleman's response has been with regard to a pattern which has now been elevated by virtue of the questioning asked to a plan. And there is no indication here of a plan, of some kind of created plan. What there is is an indication of a pattern of activity. And from what we understand, evidence of that pattern. But whether that is elevated to a plan of a particular form is not in evidence, and it is inappropriate to be calling this a plan. Unless, of course, he had a conversation with some Bosnian Serb official in which they said, Yes, we have a plan and our plan is whatever it may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this line of questioning actually spawns from the fact that Colonel Pandurevic had a map on his wall that had a very distinct line, confrontation line, decreasing the village as well as the information the colonel has provided in regards to the shelling of those outlying areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The difficulty -- the difficulty with what was just said, of course, is the interpretation. It may as well be memorialising that which is going on as anything else. There's an absence of information that is a plan. There is not an absence of information as he has testified to, that he perceived a pattern. And with regard to the issue of pattern, objectively speaking from what he saw, he saw a pattern. But that doesn't elevate itself into a plan, which is what I'm getting at. Because if there's a plan, that means that some individual or individuals got together and created such of which there is no evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, I will say indeed when you did ask the question about a plan, I almost asked you what plan is this you are talking about. I think the discussion up to that point had been about a pattern. If you could try and stick to that. And if the word "plan" had come from the witness himself for the first time, I would have gone along with you, but you seem to suggest the word. So the objection is upheld. Page 72 at line 14 to 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If I could have just one moment to consult with counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Colonel Tucker, did you discuss with either the Bosnian Serb or the Serbian leadership what you were seeing in and around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, it was the main topic of all meetings with the Bosnian Serb authorities who General Morillon met with.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At any point in time did you learn anything about these operations?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs told us that over the Orthodox new year, that Muslims out of the -- in the Srebrenica enclave had attacked Bosnian Serb villages around the enclave and had killed many villagers. Karadzic even said to General Morillon that 1.260 villagers had been killed. Karadzic in an earlier meeting in January had told General Morillon that the supply lines, the roads from Zvornik down towards Pale which had to go through some fairly narrow areas were being regularly attacked by Muslims, Muslim commandos from the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, let me stop you there. What I'm asking about, did you learn anything about the Serbian -- Bosnian Serbian operations in and around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, but it's, as with everything in Bosnia, I am afraid it's a long answer because it connects about three different things together which is what I'm trying to explain. The Serb, Bosnian Serbs said that -- sorry, Karadzic requested Morillon to investigate the disappearance of his nephew who had disappeared having left Zvornik towards Pale but had never arrived. These were given as examples by the Bosnian Serbs as to military activities and war crimes which they declared had been perpetrated by Bosnian Muslims in -- from the enclaves, and that they were attacking the enclave, and that this was deliberate in order to find the war criminals who had carried out these massacres of Bosnian Serb villagers in order to prosecute them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In your time in Srebrenica, were the villagers who were coming in to Srebrenica being held criminally or prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I am afraid I don't understand the question. The villagers were just refugees, just fleeing into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So in regards to this conversation with Karadzic that they were targeting these villages in order to make arrests, was that consistent with what you were seeing coming into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Partially. What we were seeing coming into Srebrenica were refugees fleeing from these villages which were being attacked in the way I described earlier. In all the conversation that General Morillon had with Bosnian Serb authorities about trying to get humanitarian aid into the enclaves, what the Bosnian Serb authorities said was that they would allow women, and children, and old-age men free passage out of the the enclaves at any time. However, they demanded the right to interrogate or question all men of combat age in order to satisfy themselves whether or not they had been war criminals and guilty of these attacks on the Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You mentioned previously in your transcript that you met twice more persons in Belgrade. Can you please describe the first of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The first of those meetings was with Milosevic. The second was with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please set the scene for the meeting -- well, first off, when was the first meeting with Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The meeting with Milosevic was around the 25th of March, 1992 -- sorry, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And when you met with Milosevic, was he the one and only person you saw that day?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: When we arrived at the -- at Milosevic's palace in Belgrade, there were about 20 military and other senior people present. About half were in uniform, about half were in suits. However, as we walked deeper and deeper into Milosevic's palace, guards guided more and more of these other people away so that in the end we actually sat down in a large dining room with only Milosevic and General Morillon, his body-guard, I think Thornberry was there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were you having conversations as you were being led further and further into the --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: General Morillon was speaking with Milosevic through Mihailov, his body-guard, but I was not privy to what was being said because I was walking behind them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What were the topics of conversation for that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The main topic of conversation was to ask Milosevic to exercise constraint on the Bosnian Serbs and to get the Bosnian Serbs to stop their attacks on the Srebrenica enclave, and to stop their search for revenge for the massacres that they claimed to have happened in January, and to allow humanitarian aid through to the injured and to the starving refugees in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: During your time in Srebrenica, what would have led you to believe that Milosevic could assist you in these matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, that assumes that's a fact not in evidence, which is that is a period of time in which he had such a belief. He could have had the belief before or after he ever went to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, why would you pose -- why would General Morillon have proposed these requests to Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: General Morillon believed that Milosevic as a fellow Serb would have some influence over the Bosnian Serbs. Milosevic made very clear in that meeting that he would do everything that he could, but that he had no authority or control over the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated previously that shortly after that meeting, you also had a meeting with Mladic in Belgrade. Can you please advise the Court how that came about?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That meeting came about because General Morillon also asked Milosevic to see if he could get Mladic to come to a meeting because General Morillon told Milosevic that he believed that Mladic was the Bosnian Serb with the most influence over what was happening around Srebrenica. And General Morillon requested Milosevic's assistance in getting a meeting with General Mladic. This is in the context that I mentioned a couple of hours previously that Mladic had refused or started refusing to meet with General Morillon anymore back in January. So General Morillon had not actually met with Mladic for a number of months.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How quickly was Milosevic able to accede to your request?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Milosevic's assistant told General Morillon later that evening that a meeting was being set up or had been arranged the next day in Belgrade at a villa belonging to the Belgrade government, and that a delegation from Republika Srpska would be attending, and that General Mladic would be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What did this tell you, if anything, about that relationship?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to object. It calls for speculation in so many different ways. The fact that the meeting is arranged as this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness after having numerous meetings with these individuals, is certainly able to discuss his observations as well as his opinions as to what was occurring. Thus it's not speculation. He is stating the facts as they were known to him at the time during those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The fact that a meeting is arranged between two individuals on an expedited basis when there is a perceived crisis is hardly anything that necessarily tells you about the relationship as between those two individuals. I think that the logic behind the offer of proof is lacking.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can further respond, but in doing so, I believe it may lead the witness, so I would prefer to stay in generalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that event, then I will uphold the objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, if the witness can be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In order to? I've just upheld the objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, how quickly was Milosevic able to summon Mladic, specifically?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that question has been asked and answered, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe he has a more specific answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute, wait a minute, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: She asked a specific question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just talk first, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At page 78, line 24, you asked: "How quickly was Milosevic able to accede to your request?" The witness did not answer that question. He told you how quickly he arranged the meeting. And so we don't know how quickly Milosevic acceded to the request. He probably acceded almost contemporaneously during the meeting; however, he said in his answer that the meeting was arranged for the next day, so that is how quick the meeting was arranged.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'll move on to another topic then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of the headquarters that Mladic had available to him during your time in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Again that assumes a fact not in evidence. That he had headquarters available to him. The question also is leading in nature. She can ask a proper question with regard to this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you said you were going to another topic. You want to talk about headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then that's the topic she wants to talk about, and the witness can tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The issue is headquarters available to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question says: --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well, I withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- "Are you aware of the headquarters that Mladic had available to him during your time in Bosnia?"

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But that assumes that there were headquarters available to him, and it's leading. She can say, What physical location did he have available to him at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A physical location is that he had his home available to him, he had his --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But I don't know if he did or not. He is a Bosnian Serb operating in the Republika Srpska. We are now in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But there are any number of physical locations that can be available to him --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- in Belgrade, and if the topic that she wants to talk about are headquarters, you can say -- yes, you can say that what headquarters did have available to him may be slightly leading, but the question is: Did he have any headquarters in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I misspoke myself. I misspoke myself when I said Belgrade, I should have said Bosnia. If he is aware, he can ask what he is aware of, but to lead him to what he is aware of is improper. And for purposes of getting through this, I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Because I was going to rule against it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, did you know if Ratko Mladic had headquarters available to him?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I cannot say whether or not they were headquarters. What I can say was that he had a facility available to him in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Where was this facility in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I do not know where it was in Belgrade. Mladic referred to it to Mihailov when they were speaking in Serbo-Croat and then Mihailov told me and it was -- that's one specific case where this came up. But what kind of building, what kind of facility, where it was, I had no information.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So the extent of your knowledge is that there was a facility in Belgrade somewhere, and you have no further information on that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Outside of this facility being available to Mladic, are you aware of any other links between Serbia and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't think that that question is appropriate either. What she's doing, she's asking a question with regard to what she is trying to prove, the theoretical basis of what's in her head, but there is no evidence that there's a link between Srebrenica and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm actually not even --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, excuse me, as a matter of fact, au contraire, the witness has specifically testified that in the conversations that were had with Milosevic, Milosevic indicated that he would do what he could to assist, and depending on what language one chooses to use, I believe that the gentleman used a language of seeing whether Milosevic could have individuals in the Bosnian Serb persuasion exercise constraint. So I think the issue was an issue of whether or not he could influence them in some fashion. But with regard to a link, he indicated that he had no direct control or control over them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe you can give a comprehensive answer now that you have heard the further part. I'm not sure I'm following all this.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm actually not certain if we have a relevance objection, if we have a leading objection. I am not sure what the objection is to be able to respond to it outside of a diatribe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection was that the question is not appropriate either. I'm not aware of that kind of objection unless you tell us how inappropriate the question is -- can be inappropriate because it is irrelevant, because it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The question, as presently posed Your Honour, assumes facts not in evidence. As presently posed, it is speculative, and as presently posed it is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's impossible for the response to be speculative given that he will only describe what is known to him, and he certainly was in a position to know certain occurrences. And not being relevant, given the fact that the reason we are in trial here today is in relation to Belgrade and specifically the military's involvement and actives in Republika Srpska, it certainly would be relevant. Thus, I would ask permission to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The only problem, Madam, I don't know whether this is what causes the confusion, is that you are talking about a link between Serbia and Bosnia. The link could be the Drina bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. I will choose a word beyond "link" and hopefully this will get us somewhere further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So if you talk about human beings from Bosnia and the human beings from Serbia, that might make it a little better.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, outside of this meeting set up with Mladic, are you aware of any other Serbian involvement in the operations at Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: About the 13th or 14th of March, the UN military observers who were inside the Srebrenica enclave, who I described earlier, reported seeing some aircraft, some military aircraft fly from -- over Serbia, across the Drina River, fly over Bosnia, drop bombs on two villages, and then fly back over Serbia and disappear into the distance over Serbia. That event was reported to me by two UNMOs. I then reported that event to my headquarters in Kiseljak, and I believe it was reported further up the UN chain of command. If you want specific details of that, I have them in my diary. The first aircraft was a biplane. The second two or three aircraft were monoplanes. And I can give you the grid references of the names of the villages that they dropped the bombs on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, that amount of detail will not be necessary. Were these bombs dropped within the time-period that the other villages were being shelled around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: These two particular villages which were bombed were villages on the perimeter of the Srebrenica enclave, and were subsequently captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the question, Mr. Tucker, was were these villages bombed within the time-frame that the other villages were being also attacked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, is that the only involvement that you were aware of from the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is the only factual involvement. There were other potential involvements which were reported to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What was being reported to you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We were --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, objection. Hearsay, unless it's sourced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Carry on, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, what were you learning and who were you learning it from?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We were being told by Muslim refugees of bridges being laid during the night over the Drina River and lorries being driven across these bridges and then further into Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, in visual inspections, your personal visual inspections, did you see anything that would be consistent with this story?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, before the gentleman answers that question, the word "consistent" is a dangerous word when dealing with observations. And has really very little relevance because anything can be consistent pretty much when dealing with it along those lines. So I would object at this point to the use of the terminology "consistent." If there's a fact to be established as opposed to a speculative notion with regard to an objective situation, then the question can be asked in that fashion, but the word consistent is a word which is notoriously known to be not particularly helpful when trying to deal with the proof of objective facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is merely being asked to describe what he personally saw. Again, it is not speculation, but rather his personal observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe you might want to phrase the question slightly differently to hone in on what the witness observed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, did you see anything that supported these reports?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I personally saw on the journey from Zvornik to Bratunac on our way into Srebrenica on the left-hand side of the road, in other words, the side of the road away from the Drina River, in a valley between hills, in a flat, open area, markings and tactical signage of which military use in order to line up vehicles and marshal vehicles in preparation for something. In my -- those tactical markings were similar to that which -- in my own army, the British Army, you would have marshalled large numbers of vehicles prior to moving them somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, did this area seem to be of old use or of continual use?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: There were tire marks, wheel marks in the ground, which had been left fairly recently, so it had been used fairly recently. How long previously and to what purpose, I obviously cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, as you are describing the bridges that were going over the Drina in court today --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, I apologise I'm going to object to the question at this point. That's not the testimony that's been adduced, describing the bridges going over the Drina. What you have is you have unsourced reports of something being built. And the fashion in which these questions are being asked assumes that these are now proven facts which they are not. If Ms. Carter wishes to ask the exact same question and discuss it from the standpoint of these are reports that he received, then I have no objection, but the record begins to look from the questioner's standpoint as if these are facts which are proved, and they are not, and its an inappropriate way to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, at page 85, line 24, you have an answer that says: "We were being ..." -- the transcript says "sold," but I suppose it should be "told" -- "... by Muslim refugees of bridges being laid during the night over the Drina River and lorries being driven across these bridges, and then further into Bosnia-Herzegovina." So I guess the nub of the objection is that that's what he was told? You go to keep saying according to what you were told, not -- because it's not a fact; it's what he was told.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when you were told by Muslim refugees of the bridges being laid during the the night over the Drina River, and of lorries being driven across these bridges and then further into Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you find these Muslim refugees to be reliable reporters?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the question as posed is without foundation, and that meaning, just the language on line 4, sorry, starts on line 3: "Did you find these Muslim refugees to be reliable reporters?" There's no basis for that particular question to be answered by this individual at this time, that they are reliable reporters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, the witness has indicated that this is what was reported to him, I'm merely trying to elicit whether these reports and reporters were believable. This gentleman is the one who was speaking with them and can certainly tell from his experience what did or did not appear to be reliable information to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the question of the reliability of the information is distinct from the question of the reliability of the author of the information which I'm sure Ms. Carter appreciates. That doesn't deal, of course, with the fact that he did not speak to any of these individuals, but rather there was -- any conversation that was had was a conversation that was reported to a third party at best and maybe more since he did not speak to any of these individuals directly and he has so testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which individuals directly?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The Muslim refugees, whoever they may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't know whether he did or didn't speak to them; that's not what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact we do, Your Honour. He said that he did not have direct conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness said that because he does not speak Serbo-Croat, he always used a interpreter, that's how he spoke with the refugee, specifically the body-guard of General Morillon. To say that that is somehow removed, that would be -- required that anybody sitting in the courtroom today listening to a translation could not rely upon that translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, we've been in that situation as a matter of fact in this court. A question of reliability -- the question of the reliability of the author of information is a question which requires a fair amount of analysis. But with regard to where we stand right now, there's lack of foundation with regard to the question that's been asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There is a difference, Madam Carter, between whether a statement or a person is reliable, and whether the listener believes the person. Those are two different concepts.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I will try to narrowly focus this.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, how did you learn about the laying of the bridges and the lorries coming over the Drina?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I learned about it through two sources. The first was that some of our UNMOs reported being told that by locals. And secondly was in conversation through Mihailov with some refugees as we were walking around Srebrenica. And Mihailov was asking them what were they seeing, where had they come from, had they had any food, when had they last eaten, et cetera. This came up in, and a particular refugee said that to Mihailov and Mihailov said it to me. So I heard it from two sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you believe this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, objection. Relevance as to whether he believed it or not. It's not relevant whether he believed it, he obtained the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, did you believe this information?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I believed it was plausible.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Because we in UN BH command believed that the Bosnian Serb army was incapable of carrying on operations without resupply of particularly fuel and spare parts from somewhere. We had intelligence assessments which showed that the Bosnian Serbs had huge amounts of ammunition and were not short of ammunition, but they were very short of fuel and spare parts. We frequently came across Bosnian Serb military vehicles at the side of the road just run out of fuel. And we therefore believed that they had to be getting fuel and spare parts from somewhere and the only logical place where this fuel and spare parts could possibly come from was from Serbia. So, therefore, we believed that in some way, shape, or form they had to be getting across the Drina into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicate that the only logical place where the fuel and spare parts could possibly come from was Serbia. Why is this the only plausible place?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Because they were --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, he didn't say plausible, he said logical. There is a difference. Line 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: My sincere apologies the transcript was being corrected at the point that I was trying to read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated that the only logical place for the fuel and spare parts could possibly come from was Serbia. What made you believe this?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Logic. There was a no-fly zone imposed over Serbia, so and we knew that no aircraft were flying into Bosnia. On the -- to the north, to the west, and to the south, the Bosnian Serbs were facing enemy on a front line and there was no -- obviously no resupply of any kind going across those confrontation lines. The only friendly area was to the east, to Serbia, over the Drina River. And General Mladic and all his colleagues in the Bosnian Serb Army had previously been members of the Yugoslav Army, and were therefore -- had in the -- literally a number of months previously been part of the military organisation of Serbia, and, therefore, it seemed to us highly likely that that is where they were getting resupply, particularly of fuel, but also of spare parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When speaking -- or, were you aware of any other support from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. We heard gossip from Serb -- Bosnian Serb officers that senior officers of the Bosnian Serb army continued to be paid from Belgrade throughout the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicate that this was gossip. Did you maintain the opinion that this was gossip?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We initially heard this in the margins of the various meetings that we were having. This was when Mihailov was speaking with Bosnian Serb officers and Mihailov told me afterwards that they were waiting for their money from Belgrade. When I was subsequently in the -- this is in 1996, when I was subsequently in the UK crisis management headquarters in Northward which was responsible for the provisions of UK military forces to IFOR and to SFOR, I was -- I had intelligence made available to me which showed that this was in fact the case and that the Bosnian Serb senior officers, I can't remember whether it was a rank of major upwards or whether it was a rank of colonel upwards, salaries were being paid from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to move back to your time in Srebrenica. You indicated that the people were starving and listless. Was any more aid brought to these people?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The first aid that we managed to get into Srebrenica was the beginning of December, as I had described a number of hours previously. The second aid that arrived in the enclaves came from the airdrops which started in February. However, that was fairly haphazard and extremely dangerous. The third time that -- and the airdrops carried on now and then for a number of months. The third specific time that aid arrived in Srebrenica was on a convoy of which General Morillon persuaded the Bosnian Serbs to allow through and which arrived in Srebrenica around the 17th or 18th of March, 1993. Then a further convoy arrived around the 27th or 28th, and I believe that then a number of further convoys arrived, but I left Srebrenica around the 28th of March, so don't have specific information after that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd like to focus on the convoy in which Morillon led. Can you please describe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How long are you going to be on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Oh goodness. It will take a bit of time, Your Honour. I apologise. I didn't notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would then this be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Prior to the adjournment I request that we receive copies of the intelligence that were made available to Colonel Tucker that he testified to at page 92, line 13. Since we don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break and come back tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. Same courtroom. Court adjourned. May I just say, Mr. Tucker, that while you are still in the witness-stand, you may not discuss the topic with anybody, the case with anybody, not even with your counsel. Okay. Court adjourned.
